blocks.text: It is proved that שפן saphan is not the rabbit, as they claim, but a kind of larger mouse in Eretz Yisrael, Egypt and Libya, which is called Δίπους [Dipous] by Herodotus and others, Χοιρογρύλλιος [Choirogryllios] by the Elders, Ἀρκτομῦς [Arktomys] by Jerome, and اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo by the Arabs; on which many things not yet published are reported from Arabic writings.

Levit. XI, 5. and Deut. XIV, 7. In the lists of animals that chew the cud but [col. 1002] do not have a cloven hoof, and are therefore unclean, the השפן, ὁ σαφάν [ho saphan], is enumerated together with the camel and the hare. The plural שפנים sephanim occurs in Psal. CIV. 18. The rock is a refuge לשפנים, τοῖς σεφανίμ [tois sephanim]. And Prov. XXX, 26. שפנים sephanim are a feeble people, yet they make their home in the rock. Most of the more recent writers explain it as rabbits. Many points seem at first sight to favor this interpretation. 1. In the Law, twice, השפן is joined with הארנבת, that is, with the hare, as a kindred animal. 2. The passage of the Psalm that we just cited is rendered in the Greek edition thus: Πέτρα καταφυγὴ τοῖς λαγωοῖς [Petra kataphygē tois lagōois], the rock is a refuge for hares. Some manuscripts have τοῖς χοιρογρυλλίοις [tois choirogryllois], that is, as they claim, hedgehogs. But the oldest writers follow the former reading. Jerome, Epistle 135, to Sunia and Fretela: All have rendered it χοιρογρυλλίους [choirogryllious], with a similar word; the LXX alone interpreted it as hares. Theodoret in his commentary on this Psalm, Basil on Isaiah, chapter 2, and Apollinaris in his Paraphrase also read thus:
Πέτροις ἠλιβάτοις περιθάρσεες εἰσὶ λαγωοὶ [Petrois ēlibatois peritharseis eisi lagōoi],

Hares are confident in the steep rocks; and the Arabic version, which was made from the Greek: the rock is a refuge الارانب [al-arānib] of hares. Others join both: as Augustine on this passage: The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs and hares. Arnobius: There is the rock, offering refuge either to the children of hedgehogs, etc. or to hares. Bede on Proverbs, chapter 30: And it should be noted that in the Psalm, where we sing: „The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs, in some codices hares is found, in others hedgehogs “. 3. The Hebrew of Prov. XXX, 26. שפנים עם לא עצום the Vulgate translator rendered thus: The little hare is a feeble people, following, if I am not mistaken, [II, 410] some Greek interpreter who had explained שפנים as λαγίδεις [lagideis] little hares, that is, rabbits. For in Strabo, book 3, λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, are taken for rabbits. The Greeks have no other name for the rabbit. For in Aelian κόνικλος [koniklos], in Polybius and Galen κούνικλος [kounikllos] of the Spaniards, in Strabo and Erotian λεβηρὶς [lebēris] of the people of Marseilles were their own words, not used in Greece. 4. The old Book of Names, which they ascribe to Philo, has in Jeremiah thus: SAPHAN, hedgehog, hare, or hedgehog. And in Ezekiel, SAPHAN, hedgehog, or hare. 5. In the Arabic Lexicon of Giggeius, p. 854, vol. 2, سفن [safan] saphan is rendered rabbit. Where he has this from, however, I do not know at all. For I have found it nowhere else. 6. The Hebrew name שפן saphan seems to allude to the Hebrew verbs ספן and צפן, of which the former means to cover, the latter to hide. And it seems to fit the rabbit, which seeks the hiding places of burrows, to lie concealed in them and be covered, as it were. Martial:
The rabbit delights to dwell in hollowed-out caves.
